title: Signature Clear-Room Weaver
body:
The Signature Clear-Room Weaver is an original Signature design for preparing a play space before a headset session. Instead of relying on memory, the Weaver walks the user through a spoken room check, names each hazard type in turn, and only declares the room ready when every check is answered. It is a Signature design, not a public product, and it is presented here as a design to be built and tested, not as a device you can buy.

How to do it: Speak the room check aloud, one hazard type at a time; Confirm furniture, cables, pets, and people in turn; Draw the boundary from the spoken answers, not from a guess; Require a fresh check whenever the room changes; Keep a spoken log of each cleared session for the household to review.

What to check: Test the Weaver by deliberately leaving one hazard in place and confirming it refuses to declare the room ready. A checker that passes a dirty room is worse than no checker, because it replaces vigilance with confidence.

When to stop or get help: Stop using the Weaver's approval if it ever declares a room ready that was not checked. Return to a manual foot check of the room until the design is fixed and retested.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

checks = ['furniture', 'cables', 'pets', 'people']
answers = ['clear', 'clear', 'clear', 'clear']
print('checks:', len(checks))
print('clear answers:', answers.count('clear'))
print('weaver approves:', answers.count('clear') == len(checks))

weaver approves: True

title: Signature Comfort Clock
body:
The Signature Comfort Clock is an original Signature design for break discipline in virtual reality. It counts session time in the open, announces breaks in a calm voice, and asks the user to rate comfort before allowing the session to continue. Its point is to remove the negotiation with yourself: the clock, agreed before the session, decides when you pause, so tiredness does not have to argue with enthusiasm.

How to do it: Set the break interval and the session limit before starting; Announce each break and require the headset to be removed; Ask for a comfort rating from fine to queasy at each break; End the session automatically if comfort falls twice in a row; Log comfort ratings so patterns over days become visible.

What to check: Test the Clock by setting a short interval and confirming it interrupts a gripping scene on time. A break timer that politely waits for a convenient moment is not a break timer.

When to stop or get help: Disable the design's approval if it lets sessions continue past two poor comfort ratings. Fall back to a kitchen timer and a written rule until it is repaired.

title: Signature Gentle-Motion Ladder
body:
The Signature Gentle-Motion Ladder is an original Signature design for building motion tolerance step by step. It ranks movement types from gentlest to strongest, starts every new user at the bottom, and only unlocks the next rung after a comfortable session on the current one. It treats tolerance as something earned over days, not something to be forced in one afternoon.

How to do it: Rank movement types from still scenes to smooth gliding; Start every new user at the gentlest rung; Require one comfortable session before unlocking the next rung; Step back down a rung after any queasy session; Keep a personal ladder record so progress is visible and setbacks are normal.

What to check: Test the Ladder by trying to skip rungs and confirming it refuses. A ladder that lets enthusiasm override its own order is decoration, not a safety design.

When to stop or get help: Return to the gentlest rung if queasiness appears at a higher rung, and stay there until comfort returns for a full session. Do not climb while ill in the hope of adapting.

title: Signature Young-User Gate
body:
The Signature Young-User Gate is an original Signature design that makes supervision structural rather than advisory. It asks for the device maker's age guidance, the content check, and a named adult in the room before a young user's session can start, and it shortens sessions automatically for young users. It is a design for households that want the gate to hold even when the adult is busy and the child is persuasive.

How to do it: Require age guidance, content check, and a named adult before starting; Shorten young-user sessions automatically; Require an adult to confirm each break; Log who supervised each session; Refuse to start if any gate check is missing.

title: Signature Street-Sense Overlay
body:
The Signature Street-Sense Overlay is an original Signature design for augmented reality walking. It deliberately fades overlays at crossings, stairs, and junctions, replaces visual directions with short audio prompts, and shows a bold stop reminder when the user approaches a road. Its philosophy is that an overlay should get out of the way precisely when the real world gets dangerous, not compete with it.

How to do it: Fade overlays to a minimum at crossings, stairs, and junctions; Switch to short audio directions while walking; Show a stop reminder before every road crossing; Restore the full overlay only when the user has stopped in a safe place; Log every fade event so the design can be audited.

What to check: Test the Overlay on a quiet street walk and count how many crossings it faded for. If it fades for none, it is a decoration, not a safety design, and should not be trusted on a busy street.

When to stop or get help: Stop using the Overlay for walking if it ever fails to fade at a crossing. Walk with the device put away until the design is fixed.

title: Signature Flash Guard
body:
The Signature Flash Guard is an original Signature design that screens virtual scenes for rapid flashing and high-contrast alternating patterns before they play. When it finds a risky scene, it offers a safe alternative: a slowed version, a still description, or a skip. It never asks a photosensitive user to test a scene to find out whether it is risky; screening happens before exposure, not during it.

How to do it: Scan each scene for flashing and rapid alternating patterns before play; Flag risky scenes and offer a slowed, still, or skip alternative; Keep a personal list of flagged titles; Warn other household members when a flagged title is opened; Allow a clinician's note to tighten the screening for one person.

What to check: Test the Guard with a known flashing test scene and confirm it flags it before play. A guard that only warns after the scene has started has failed its purpose.

When to stop or get help: Stop trusting the Guard if a flashing scene ever plays without a flag. Avoid flashing content entirely until the screening is repaired and retested.

title: Signature Eye-Ease Fitter
body:
The Signature Eye-Ease Fitter is an original Signature design for headset fitting. It guides the user through lens spacing, headset level, and text size with a sharpness test at each step, and it refuses to declare the fit good until text reads clearly in both eyes. It treats a blurry fit as an unfinished setup, not as something to tolerate for the sake of starting quickly.

How to do it: Guide lens spacing with a sharpness test in each eye; Check headset level and pressure on brow and cheeks; Set text size for comfortable reading; Retest sharpness after turning the head; Store one fit profile per person and reload it on each use.

What to check: Test the Fitter by deliberately mis-setting the lens spacing and confirming it reports blur. A fitter that approves every setting is not measuring anything.

When to stop or get help: Stop using a stored fit profile if it ever produces blur or eye pain. Refit from scratch and, if pain persists, seek eye care.

title: Signature Room Sentinel
body:
The Signature Room Sentinel is an original Signature design that watches the play space while the user cannot. It announces when someone enters the room, when a pet crosses the boundary, and when a cable has moved into the play area, using sound rather than a visual warning the wearer cannot see. Its job is to be the eyes the headset takes away.

How to do it: Announce visitors, pets, and moved objects by sound; Pause the session automatically if someone enters the play space; Keep a spoken log of interruptions; Resume only after the user confirms the space is clear again; Work even when the virtual scene is loud, by ducking its audio for warnings.

When to stop or get help: Stop relying on the Sentinel if it ever misses an entry. Return to a guarded room with a human watcher until it is repaired.

title: Signature Quiet-Room Privacy
body:
The Signature Quiet-Room Privacy design is an original Signature approach to shared virtual spaces. Before entering, it shows exactly what will be shared: voice range, camera view, tracking data, and recording status, in plain words. It defaults to the most private setting and requires a deliberate choice to share more, rather than defaulting to open and requiring the user to hunt for privacy.

How to do it: Show sharing settings in plain words before entering; Default microphone, camera, and tracking to the most private option; Require a deliberate choice to share more; Warn before any recording starts; Offer a one-tap private room for sensitive conversations.

What to check: Test the design by entering a shared space and confirming the defaults are private without any changes. If the defaults are open, the design has failed, however good its settings menu looks.

When to stop or get help: Leave any space at once if recording starts without warning, or if private settings change without your choice. Report the incident through the platform's tools.

title: Signature Task-Lock
body:

When it detects driving, cycling, or machinery operation, it locks the headset display and shows only a plain instruction to stop the task first. title: Signature Household Safety Covenant
body:
The Signature Household Safety Covenant is an original Signature design for turning household headset rules into a living agreement. It records the play space, the stop word, break rules, supervisors, and fit profiles in one place, reviews them after any incident, and suspends sessions automatically when the agreement lapses. It treats safety as a household contract, not as one person's memory.

How to do it: Record space, stop word, break rules, supervisors, and fit profiles together; Review the agreement after any incident; Suspend sessions if the agreement lapses or a review is overdue; Let any household member call a pause; Keep the agreement visible where headsets are stored.

title: Signature Comfort Audit Engine
body:
The Signature Comfort Audit Engine is an original Signature design that tests comfort settings systematically instead of by guesswork. It tries one setting change at a time in a calm scene, records a comfort score for each, and recommends the combination with the best score. It keeps a history per person, so a setting that helped last month is not lost when a new app resets everything.

How to do it: Test one setting change at a time in a calm scene; Record a comfort score for each combination; Recommend the best-scoring combination; Keep a per-person history across apps; Restore the best profile when a new app resets settings.

What to check: Test the Engine by changing two settings at once in a trial and confirming it warns that the result cannot be attributed. An audit that changes everything at once cannot teach anything.

When to stop or get help: Reset to the known best profile if a new app makes you ill despite the audit. Report the app's behaviour with your profile noted.

title: Signature Fall-Response Protocol
body:
The Signature Fall-Response Protocol is an original Signature design for what happens after a fall or collision. It removes the headset view, speaks calm instructions, asks simple check questions about pain, dizziness, and confusion, and writes a plain incident note. It does not diagnose: it structures the first minutes so that panic does not decide what happens next, and it insists on medical help for warning signs.

How to do it: Remove the headset view and speak calm instructions; Ask about pain, dizziness, and confusion in plain words; Write a plain incident note with time and cause; Flag warning signs and urge prompt medical help; Block further sessions that day after a flagged incident.

title: Signature Session Balance Ledger
body:
The Signature Session Balance Ledger is an original Signature design that treats session time, breaks, wind-down, and sleep as one budget. It shows the day's total, warns before evening sessions that would eat into wind-down time, and records patterns over weeks. Its aim is not to police fun, but to make the trade-off visible: a long late session is a choice about tomorrow's sleep, made with eyes open.

title: Signature Demo-Day Safety Kit
body:

It bundles a supervisor checklist, a cleaning routine, a per-person fitting check, short session timers, and a watch-without-wearing option into one kit that a demo station cannot open without completing.
